I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen

Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

I have to be on guard all the time

issues.explanation: 'Shouting in Arabic' is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of stalking unless there is specific trauma detail indicating the stalker used Arabic; with the rest of the profile, this trigger appears overly specific and disconnected from the other stalking-related items.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: 'I can talk about what happened very easily' conflicts with the same Memory node items describing fragmented, intrusive, partially inaccessible trauma memory ('extremely clear while others are completely blank' and 'fragments appear suddenly without warning'). While not impossible, this is a direct enough tension within the node to question coherence.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: Fear of losing control of anger and doing something terrible is poorly integrated with the rest of the profile, which centers on fear, mistrust, stranger threat, and life damage after stalking. It points toward a perpetration/harm-to-others concern not otherwise represented in Threat, Triggers, Memory, or strategies, making the formulation less coherent.

vignette: Clara, a twenty-eight-year-old teacher, had always valued quiet routines until the autumn the stalking began. It started when a man followed her home after school, his footsteps syncing with hers until she turned a corner into a dimly lit alley. When she finally stopped, the heavy breathing sounds echoing from behind a dumpster made her stomach drop; she froze, certain he was still there, just out of sight. Those immediate sensations of being followed and the auditory cue of heavy breathing would instantly flood her body with strong negative emotions like fear and horror. Because those triggers kept forcing her to re-live the violation, she had come to believe that people fundamentally couldn’t be trusted, and that her life had been thoroughly destroyed by the trauma. In the weeks that followed, the trauma’s partial clarity left her stranded between sharp flashbacks and total amnesia. She knew exactly what had happened, yet she remained unable to find words to describe it, and that wordless confusion would cascade into a fresh wave of terror. Whenever fragments of the memory appeared suddenly without warning, they would automatically activate her sensitivity to heavy breathing and the feeling of being tracked. The sheer weight of those negative emotions would then make the silence around her feel dangerous; unusual silence in her empty apartment or a quiet school hallway after the final bell made her certain she was about to be hurt again. Because she believed she had to be on guard all the time, her own hypervigilance constantly scanned for police cars and the sensation of being followed, turning ordinary street corners into active triggers. Now teaching third grade, Clara navigated a classroom that felt perpetually unstable. Her conviction that her life was ruined ensured that each new threat from strangers approaching her in ordinary situations immediately ignited intense shame and anger. When she felt threatened by a stranger in the school parking lot, that spike of alarm would immediately turn her attention toward authority presence outside the gates. The intense dread she felt in that moment would pull another fragmented piece of the stalking into her consciousness, and the partial clarity of the event—where specific moments stayed sharp while other hours vanished—would only deepen her negative appraisal that her life was destroyed. She had come to believe that if she stopped monitoring the perimeter, the stalking would resume, so she kept her hypervigilance as her daily armor. Clara’s relationship had borne the quiet strain of her withdrawal. Her partner often noticed how she would flinch at ordinary noises or how she would retreat into silence when the house grew too quiet, fearing that the stillness masked something dangerous. At first, she told herself this was just survival, but the exhaustion of maintaining her guard around her classroom doors and down her own hallway had begun to outweigh any sense of protection. What frightened her most was not the stalking itself, but the realization that she could no longer trust her own environment or her own mind to keep her safe. She had come to therapy hoping to find a way to quiet the internal alarm that had fired since that alley, though she worried that speaking it out loud might only make the fragmented memories sharper, and that her life might never be the same again.
